summary: Describes a process experiment under RFC 3933 that temporarily changed the criteria for volunteers to qualify for the IETF Nominating Committee. It made the criteria more flexible given growing remote participation, and also changed the criteria for signing community recall petitions. It was replaced by RFC 9389.

plainLanguage.summary: The rules for who may help pick IETF leaders were tweaked as a trial, because more people were joining from home.

questions: who can volunteer for the ietf nomcom
subtitle: Temporary expanded paths for volunteers to lead IETF governance

tldr.problem: With many IETF meetings cancelled and increasing remote participation, traditional rules requiring attendance at three of the last five meetings in person shut out capable remote-only participants from the Nominating Committee that selects IETF leadership.
tldr.mechanism: The experiment added two alternative paths: service as a Working Group Chair or Secretary in the last 3 years, or authorship of at least two IETF Stream RFCs in the last 5 years. Any qualifying path grants eligibility.
tldr.outcome: This was an experiment of fixed duration (one or two nominating cycles in 2021-2022) that was replaced by RFC 9389, which made permanent changes to the qualification rules.

facts.label: Path 2 window
facts.value: 3 years of WG Chair or Secretary service

today: RFC 8989 was an Experimental process experiment that was replaced by RFC 9389, which established permanent changes to NomCom eligibility rules in 2023. The three-path approach proved workable, and RFC 9389 refined and formalized these rules in the standards.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 8713 defined how the IETF Nominating Committee (NomCom) and community recall process work. At the core of that RFC was a single criterion for eligibility: a volunteer must have registered for and attended three out of the last five IETF plenary meetings.

When IETF 107 through 110 were cancelled or moved online, this criterion became impossible or impractical. RFC 8989 created a time-limited experiment to fix this by offering alternative paths to eligibility, tailored to the shift toward remote participation. The same flexible criteria also applied to who could sign community recall petitions.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally, to help pick IETF leaders you had to show up to meetings in person. When meetings went online, that rule stopped working, so they tried new rules that let remote workers help.

sections.title: Duration and Evaluation
sections.content:
This experiment applied to the IETF Nominating Committee cycle that started in 2021. It could last for one or two consecutive nominating committee cycles (roughly one to two years), after which the IESG and community would evaluate the results and decide whether to make permanent changes, try a different approach, or revert to the original rules.

The IESG was required to consult with both the sitting NomCom Chair and the previous NomCom Chair, publish a report on the experiment's success, and begin a community discussion about what comes next. Points to evaluate included whether the new criteria produced a sufficiently large and diverse volunteer pool, and whether all stated goals had been met.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rules were a trial run that would last a year or two. Then the leaders would check if it worked, and decide whether to keep the new rules, try something else, or go back to the old way.

sections.title: The Three Qualifying Paths
sections.content:
Any person could qualify through one of three alternative paths (unless they were disqualified under other rules):

Path 1 was the traditional meeting attendance rule, updated: attend three out of the last five IETF meetings. For online-only meetings, online registration and attendance now counted; for hybrid meetings, only attendance at the registered event counted (not remote attendance at a face-to-face meeting). For the 2021-2022 NomCom, the relevant meetings were IETF 106, 107, 108, 109, and 110.

Path 2 gave eligibility to anyone who had served as a Working Group Chair or Secretary within the 3 years prior to the call for volunteers. This path recognized active contribution to IETF work through formal leadership roles.

Path 3 covered those who were listed authors or editors of at least two IETF Stream RFCs in the last 5 years. Internet-Drafts approved by the IESG and waiting in the RFC Editor queue counted the same as published RFCs, using the date the draft reached the queue. This path recognized deep technical contribution over a longer time window, since IETF documents often take 3 to 4 years to publish.
sections.plainLanguage: You could qualify three ways: show up to meetings (in person or on video), lead a working group in the last 3 years, or write 2 official IETF documents in the last 5 years. Any one was enough.

sections.title: Implementation and Data
sections.content:
All required data for evaluating the paths existed in IETF systems: the Secretariat kept meeting attendance records, and the IETF Datatracker maintained records of Working Group leaders and RFC authors. The Secretariat could evaluate eligibility mechanically and then review the results for consistency (since databases occasionally contained duplicates or alternate name spellings).

Analysis performed in August 2020 (before the experiment) showed the expansion's scope. Path 1 alone would qualify about 806 people (after disqualifications). Paths 2 and 3 combined would add about 1509 more eligible people. Roughly 30 percent of those eligible via Path 1 were also eligible via Path 2 or 3; many qualified through unique paths. A separate Path (service in the IESG or IAB) was evaluated but rejected because historical data showed such people always qualified through another path.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF kept records of meetings, working group leaders, and document authors, so they could check eligibility automatically. Tests showed this would let a lot more people qualify, especially those who did background work without attending every meeting.

sections.title: Goals and Omitted Criteria
sections.content:
The experiment aimed to mitigate disenfranchisement of remote participants, enable a representative NomCom when in-person attendance was impossible, prepare for a future of less-frequent face-to-face meetings, ensure continued understanding of IETF practices, and use automated criteria that the Secretariat could verify.

Several criteria were rejected during community discussion: authorship of individual or Working-Group-adopted Internet-Drafts, email participation, draft review, BOF chair roles, and external liaison service. These were found to be either less reliable indicators of IETF knowledge or unlikely to significantly expand the volunteer pool. No qualitative evaluation of individual contributions was considered, since the criteria had to be mechanically verifiable.
sections.plainLanguage: The three paths were picked to catch people with real IETF knowledge. The experiment ignored looser signs like email activity or reviewing drafts, because those are harder to measure fairly and don't guarantee someone understands how the IETF works.
